# Documentation {#sec-documentation}

Good documentation is essential for transparency, collaboration,
reproducibility, and long-term usability of scientific software and
data science projects. Documentation is not only a description of the
code or data, but also a guide for users and contributors to
understand the purpose, structure, and usage of the repository. For
example, it also includes licensing information, citation metadata,
and contribution guidelines.

In a code project, documentation is typically organized into two main
categories:
1. **Code documentation**: This includes inline comments, docstrings,
   and notebooks that explain the functionality of the code, its
   inputs and outputs, and any relevant details for users and
2. **Repository documentation**: This includes files like README.md,
   CHANGELOG.md, and CONTRIBUTING.md that provide an overview of the
   project, its purpose, how to use it, and how to contribute.
   developers.

Besides these two main categories, documentation can also include
tutorials, examples, and other resources that help users and
contributors understand and use the repository effectively.


## Code documentation (comments, docstrings, notebooks)

In @sec-goodcoding, we discussed the importance of writing clean,
efficient, and maintainable code. However, even well-written code can be
difficult to understand without proper documentation. Code documentation
serves as a bridge between the code and its users, providing context,
explanations, and guidance for understanding and using the code
effectively.

You can document your code in several ways. You can use inline
comments to explain specific lines or blocks of code. You can use
docstrings to provide detailed explanations of functions, classes,
and modules. You can also use notebooks to combine code, narrative,
and output in a single document, making it easier to follow the logic
and results of your analysis.


### Code comments

When reading code, you often must guess what was inside the head of
the developer who wrote it. When writing code it is important to keep
in mind that others (and your future self) will read it. Comments are
a way to communicate your thought process, intentions, and decisions.
This valuable information is otherwise lost. Only the code and a lot
guessing remains.

Comments take space and time to read. So it is better if
it is actually worth reading. When writing comments it is important to
realise what not to comment. If the code is self-explanatory, comments
are not needed. For example in the next code snippet:

```r
# Generate 100 random numbers from a normal distribution
random_numbers <- rnorm(100)  
# Calculate the average of the random numbers
average <- mean(random_numbers)  

```

If you have any clue about R code, it is obvious what the code does.
So it is better not to comment this code.

Also, comments should not explain bad written code. For example to
explain a badly named variable:

```r
x <- c(1:5)
# x record id from dataset

```

In the above example, x could be better named as record_id.

With a comment you can record your thoughts. @boswell_art_2012
suggest to see comments as "director commentary" in a movie. The director
can explain why a scene is shot in a certain way, or why a certain actor
was chosen. In the same way, you can explain your code with comments.

For example, if we reuse the example of the previous chapter, we can
add comments to explain the code:

```r
variables <- c("Petal.Width", "Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")

# Fit linear models for each variable in the iris dataset. For
# performance reasons, we use lapply. A for loop was to slow.
models <- lapply(variables, function(var) {
  lm(Petal.Length ~ get(var), data = iris)
})

# We assign names to the list of models so we can reference them
# easily later.
names(models) <- variables
```

Code comments can also help during code review. For example, if you
tried several approaches to solve a problem, you can comment that the
chose approach was the best one, and why. This can help reviewers
understand why you made certain decisions and provide feedback on your
approach.

Code comments can also be used to paint the big picture of your project. I
you have a complex project with multiple scripts, functions, etcetera,
then you also have a conceptual model. (REF chapter concept model) When
painting the big picture, you can explain how the different parts of the
project fit together by referring to the conceptual model. For example,
for a data tidying script:

```r
# This is the data tidying script for the project. It takes raw data
# prepared in the import script and tidy this data so it can be used by
# the analysis script.

result <- do_a_lot_of_data_tidy_stuff(data)
```

If you need to write a lot of commentary, than maybe you should
consider writing a notebook instead of a script.

### Notebooks

In a notebook you can combine code, narrative, and output in a single document, making it
easier to follow the logic and results of your analysis. Notebooks are
especially useful for data exploration, analysis, and visualization,
as they allow you to document your thought process and findings
alongside the code that produced them. Notebooks can be converted into
other formats, like html pages or pdf documents. This makes it also
easier to share your work with others who may not be familiar with the
programming language or environment you are using. If someone asks you
to perform a certain analysis, you can send them a notebook with the
code and the results, so they can see exactly what you did and how you
did it. You can even hide the code and only show the results, if you
want to. 

Writing a notebook in R is different then writing a notebook in
Python. In R, you can use R Markdown (.Rmd) or Quarto to create
notebooks. In Python, you can
use Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb) to achieve the same goal. Both tools
allow you to include text, images, and other media alongside your
code, making it easier to explain your analysis and results. It goes
to far to explain how to write a notebook in this book. For more
information, see the [R Markdown](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/) and
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) documentation for R, and the [Jupyter
Notebook](https://jupyter.org/) documentation for Python.

A notebook can also be considered code, but with a lot of
documentation. Therefore, notebooks should also be under
version control and reviewed by others.

### Docstrings

Docstrings are a way to document functions, classes, and modules in a
structured and standardized format. They provide a clear and concise
description of the purpose, parameters, return values, and exceptions
of a function or class, making it easier for users and contributors to
understand how to use the code effectively. Docstrings are typically
placed at the beginning of a function or class definition. 

In R docstrings are written using the
[roxygen2](https://roxygen2.r-lib.org/) package, which allows you to
write documentation in a simple and readable format. Roxygen2 uses
special tags to indicate the purpose of the function, its parameters,
return values, and any exceptions that may be raised. The
documentation is then automatically generated from the roxygen2
comments and can be included in the package documentation. Even if you
are not creating a package, you can use roxygen2 to document your
functions. The documentation will be generated in the main folder of
your project. When you move your functions into a package, the
documentation will be included. For more information about using
roxygen2 in packages, see the [Function
Documentation](https://r-pkgs.org/man.html) chapter of the R Packages
book by Hadley Wickham. 

In Python, docstrings are written using triple
quotes (""" or ''') and follow the [PEP 257
conventions](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/). The docstring should
be placed immediately after the function or class definition and
should provide a clear and concise description of the purpose,
parameters, return values, and exceptions of the function or class

## Repository documentation (README, CHANGELOG, CONTRIBUTING)

The RIVM sets clear standards and minimum
requirements for documentation in Git repositories, with a focus on
[open source](https://opensource.org/osd) This section describes those
standards and provides practical guidance.

Repository documentation helps users and contributors understand, use, and maintain your repository.
At the RIVM, the following files are required when publish the Git repository and are strongly encourage for internal repositories:

-   🏷️ README.md: Provides an overview of the repository, its purpose, and how to use it. Should include:
    -   Project or repository objectives and description
    -   Instructions for installation and use
    -   Folder structure explanation
    -   Example commands or workflows
    -   Contact details and links to further resources
    -   References to publications, datasets, or related work (with persistent identifiers) where possible
    -   Information about the computational environment (which files to use for setup: requirements.txt, renv.lock, etc.)
-   📅 CHANGELOG.md: Keeps a log of changes to the repository, including new features, fixes, improvements, and version numbers. Best practices:
    -   Use semantic versioning (e.g., 1.0.0) or year-based versioning (e.g., 2024.1)
    -   Clearly describe changes for each release
    -   Place the CHANGELOG in the root of the repository
    -   Follow the [Keep a Changelog style guide](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/)
-   🤝 CONTRIBUTING.md: Explains how others can contribute, report issues, and suggest improvements. Should address:
    -   Guidelines for submitting issues, merge/pull requests
    -   Coding standards and review process
    -   How to contact maintainers or admins
    -   Reference to the Code of Conduct
    -   Data policies (e.g., do not upload sensitive data, use mock/example data for demonstration)
    -   Any domain-specific quality assurance steps or required checks before publication
-   ⚖️ LICENSE: Describes how others may use, modify, or distribute the work. Important to keep in mind
    -   Code cannot be reused if no license exists in the repository.
    -   We recommend the use of open licenses for software such as the [EULP v1.2](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/eupl-1.2/) and compatible licenses (e.g., Apache, GNU GPL or MIT) depending on the situation for reusability of the repository
    -   Check <https://choosealicense.com/> or contact the data stewards for questions about open licenses.
-   📝 CITATION.cff A machine-readable file providing citation metadata to allow others to properly reference your repository in academic publications or reports. This is one way to present your metadata information:
    -   You can create the CITATION file easily using [ccfinit](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/#/), as explained in this video from the eScience Center: [How to create a CITATION.cff using cffinit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zcgLIT5Qd4M).

## Example scripts and tutorials

- Examples and Tutorials:
  - Provide example scripts, walkthroughs, or notebooks in a /docs or /examples folder.
  - Clearly indicate where users should start.
  - If your repository includes computational environments or dependencies, reference these in the documentation so users know how to set up and run your code (see also @sec-reproducible)


## Keeping documentation up-to-date
Documentation is only useful if it reflects the current state of the project. Make updating documentation part of your development workflow:

- Update documentation files (README, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG, etc.) whenever code, data, or project structure changes.
- Review documentation regularly for relevance and completeness, especially before major releases or sharing the repository publicly.
- Encourage all contributors to help maintain and improve documentation, and treat documentation changes as part of the code review process.
- Reference documentation status and update needs in your version control workflow (for example, linking issues or merge requests to documentation tasks).

By maintaining clear, accurate, and up-to-date documentation throughout
your software/project development life cycle, you ensure your work is
compliant with RIVM and open science standards, and ready for effective
collaboration and future reuse.
